opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing, honestly, is a kind of deep curiosity paired with taste. A lot of people can run experiments, but the people who really stand out have an intuition for which questions are worth asking. They look at a model's behavior and think, "That's weird, why is it doing that?" and then follow that thread instead of moving on.

The second thing is being comfortable across the whole stack. On a team like mine, the line between research and engineering is blurry. You might spend the morning on a new evaluation idea, the afternoon debugging a data pipeline, and the evening on a quick prototype so people can feel what the model is like to interact with. The people who thrive don't think of any of that as beneath them or outside their job. They just want to make the thing work.

Related to that is speed of iteration. I really value people who can go from idea to signal quickly: a small experiment, a scrappy eval, a prototype. Then they're honest about what the signal says, even when it's not what they hoped. Intellectual honesty matters a lot. It's easy to fool yourself with a cherry-picked example, especially with language models where outputs are so persuasive.

I also look for product sense, which might be a bit unusual for research. A lot of my work has been about how models actually show up for people, things like how they behave, how they collaborate, what the interaction feels like. So I love researchers who think about the end user and can imagine new interfaces or new ways of working with models, not just pushing a benchmark number.

And finally, low ego and high agency. The field moves so fast that the best people are willing to be wrong in public, share half-baked ideas early, and take ownership of a problem without waiting for permission. If someone has that mix of curiosity, taste, scrappiness and care for the people using the model, I'm usually pretty excited to work with them.

r001.rationale: The response says she values researchers who consider end users and imagine new interfaces and ways of working with models, connecting model research with product building.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I look for is taste. Which sounds vague, but I mean something pretty specific: can this person look at a model's output and tell when something is subtly off? A lot of the work we do, especially on the post-training and evals side, is less about having the cleverest architecture idea and more about noticing. Noticing that the model is being sycophantic in a way that isn't captured by the metric. Noticing that a benchmark is saturated and no longer telling you anything. People who have that sensitivity tend to generate much better research questions than people who are just optimizing a number.

The second thing is what I'd call end-to-end ownership. In this field the line between research and engineering is basically gone. The person who has the idea for a new training signal also needs to be able to build the data pipeline, run the ablations, debug the infra when it falls over at 2 a.m., and then write up what they learned clearly enough that the rest of the team can act on it. I'm wary of people who want to only do the "ideas" part. The ideas are cheap. The execution is where you find out whether the idea was any good.

Third is a kind of intellectual honesty about negative results. So much of what we try doesn't work, and the people who are really valuable are the ones who can say quickly, "this didn't do what I thought, here's what I actually learned," rather than torturing the experiment until it confesses. That requires some ego security. You have to be okay being wrong in public a lot.

And then there's a product sensibility that I think is underrated in research hiring. A lot of my background is on the design and product side, and I've found that researchers who actually use the model, who sit with it like a user would and feel the frustration when it does something dumb, end up pointing their research at problems that matter. The ones who only ever interact with it through eval harnesses sometimes build very elegant solutions to things nobody cares about.

What I care less about than people expect: publications, pedigree, having worked at a specific lab. Some of the best people I've worked with came from pretty nontraditional paths. I'd much rather see a weird side project where someone fine-tuned a model to do something strange and wrote a thoughtful blog post about what surprised them. That tells me way more about how they think than a NeurIPS paper where they were fourth author.

So if I had to compress it: curiosity that's actually grounded in looking at data, the ability to build the whole thing yourself, honesty about what's not working, and enough taste to know which problems are worth your time.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly values product sensibility in research hires and says researchers should use the model like a user and direct research toward problems that matter.

astra-6.text:
I look for curiosity and a strong sense of ownership. Research is ambiguous—you don’t always get a clearly defined problem or know whether an idea will work. So I value people who can ask good questions, turn those questions into experiments, and learn from the results, even when they contradict their initial intuition.

For research engineers, that also means being able to build and iterate quickly while being thoughtful about what you’re measuring. For research scientists, I’m interested in how they choose problems and reason about uncertainty. There’s a lot of overlap. And across both roles, I really value people who communicate clearly and are willing to change their minds.

r001.rationale: The response mentions building and iterating quickly for research engineers, but does not say Karina seeks hires who connect model development with building products.

sol-6.1.text:
I look for curiosity and a strong sense of ownership. Research involves a lot of ambiguity, so I really value people who can take an unclear question, turn it into an experiment, and learn something useful even when the experiment doesn’t work.

I also care about judgment: Can you distinguish an interesting result from a misleading one? Can you change your mind when the evidence points somewhere else? And then communication matters a lot. You should be able to explain what you tried, what you learned, and what you’re still uncertain about so the whole team can build on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curiosity, ownership, judgment, and communication, but does not say that research hires should connect model development with building products.
